plain: Years before the Titanic sank, a novel told of a giant, supposedly unsinkable liner called the Titan that strikes an iceberg in the North Atlantic on an April night and goes down. The book is Futility, or The Wreck of the Titan, by Morgan Robertson, published in 1898. Michels brings it up himself on several episodes, as a case of a story that seems to see the future, and the researcher Eric Wargo raises it too, citing his own book Time Loops, about the idea that the mind can sense events ahead of time. Michels does not always tell it the same way: once he gives no author or title and puts the book in the early twentieth century, about ten years before the Titanic, and once he says about twelve years, where the record has 1898. If the match is more than chance, it would mean a writer somehow drew on a disaster still to come. The novel's own words, in the 1912 edition that is the text checked here, call the Titan "the largest craft afloat," "practically unsinkable," and say she "carried as few boats as would satisfy the laws"; it is "April," and the lookout cries "Iceberg. Right under the bows." That 1912 text carries both an 1898 and a 1912 copyright, and whether the 1898 first edition is worded exactly the same is not checked.
